analysis.one_liner: Doubles the maximum Pell Grant, paid for by rolling back tax breaks for wealthy estates.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died with the Congress, having attracted zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the maximum federal Pell Grant to $10,000 a year and made more low-income families automatically eligible for the maximum need-based aid. To pay for it, it would have repealed the higher alternative minimum tax exemption and ended the doubled estate and gift tax exemption years early — both tax breaks from the 2017 tax law that benefit high-income households and large estates. It also would have required colleges to publish graduation, debt, and employment-outcome data, and penalized states that cut their higher education budgets.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and middle-income college students. Pell-eligible students would see their maximum grant roughly double to $10,000 for the 2019-2020 school year, with automatic increases after that, and students from families at or below 250% of the poverty line would be automatically treated as having zero expected family contribution — meaning maximum aid and a much simpler aid application. Students would also get standardized data on graduation rates, average debt, and salaries after graduation to compare colleges before borrowing.

how_it_helps.text: Sets the maximum Pell Grant at $10,000 for the 2019-2020 award year and indexes it upward each year after that — roughly double the grant available under then-current law.

Automatically treats students from families with income at or below 250% of the federal poverty line as having a zero expected family contribution, which qualifies them for the maximum grant and cuts the paperwork they must file.

Requires every college taking federal money to post on its homepage a standard set of performance indicators — graduation rates broken out by income and race, average debt at graduation, average salary three years after graduation, and a cohort repayment rate — so prospective students can see outcomes before enrolling.
Uses the revenue from repealing the 2017 tax law's expanded AMT exemption and accelerated estate tax exemption to fund the grant increase, so the expansion is fully paid for rather than borrowed.

analysis.who_pays: High-income households and large estates. Repealing the higher alternative minimum tax exemption would raise taxes on taxpayers whose income triggers the AMT, and ending the doubled estate and gift tax exemption on enactment rather than in 2026 would restore the lower estate tax exemption for people dying or giving gifts after the bill's enactment. States that let their higher education funding fall below a 10-year average would also face a cost: schools in those states would become ineligible to receive Pell Grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wealthy estates and high-income AMT taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The state maintenance-of-effort penalty is blunt: if a state's higher education spending falls below its 10-year average, every school in that state — and every student attending one — would lose Pell eligibility entirely, punishing students for decisions made by their state legislators. The waiver process covers only exceptional circumstances like natural disasters.

The pay-fors are not purely aimed at the very rich: the alternative minimum tax exemption rollback would reach upper-middle-income taxpayers, particularly in high-tax states, whose incomes are swept into the AMT.

Colleges would take on a significant new reporting burden — dozens of disaggregated data points, employment tracking, and alumni surveys — though the bill provides extra funding and a higher per-student fee to help small institutions under 5,000 students collect the data.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: roughly doubling the Pell Grant for low-income students, funded by rolling back two tax breaks for wealthy households and estates. The main design flaw is the state funding penalty, which could cut off aid to the very students the bill is meant to help if their state government cuts budgets; the transparency rules are a modest, well-funded ask of colleges. On balance a favorable trade for working families, but the bill never gained enough support even within its sponsor's own party to be seriously considered.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee for the rest of the Congress without a hearing, a markup, or a vote, and expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Heinrich introduced the bill on September 12, 2019; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor — the cosponsor count stayed at zero for the bill's entire life.
The Finance Committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever recorded, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy estates and high-income taxpayers subject to the alternative minimum tax kept the 2017 tax law's expanded exemptions, and colleges faced no new disclosure requirements or state funding penalties. Students received no grant increase.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy households; colleges avoided new disclosure rules

for.name: Sen. Martin Heinrich
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Chuck Grassley, R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 12, 2019 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred to reveal a partisan split; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, suggesting it never became a priority for either caucus.

industries.note: The bill's pay-fors — repealing the higher AMT exemption and ending the doubled estate and gift tax exemption early — would directly raise taxes on high-income taxpayers and inheritances. Their loss is exactly what funds the Pell expansion for students.

Schools would collect more Pell revenue per low-income student, but would have to publish detailed outcome data on their homepages and could lose all Pell funds if their state cut higher education spending. The disclosure rules cut against institutions with poor results.

States would have to keep higher education spending at or above their 10-year average or every school in the state would lose Pell eligibility. The design is meant to stop states from shifting college costs onto students, but the penalty falls on students first.

Mandatory homepage disclosure of graduation rates, average debt, post-graduation salaries, and cohort repayment rates would expose institutions whose students borrow heavily and earn little — a segment where for-profit schools are overrepresented.
